prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth strip supports a coarse room layout: walls, curtains, shelving, chairs, plants and people are separated into nearer bright regions and farther dark regions, with the rear wall and window area roughly 3–5 m from the camera wearer and foreground furniture/plants roughly 0.5–2 m away. Across the five frames the viewpoint turns right; a person appears low in front-right at roughly 1–2 m in frame 4 and becomes much larger and brighter at the right edge in frame 5, suggesting approach to within about 0.5–1 m, while another partial bright human-shaped region at the extreme right may be similarly close. It also exposes occlusion and proximity more clearly than RGB: foreground people and curtains block parts of the wall, and the nearest person is partly outside the bottom and right image boundaries. Metric distances remain highly approximate because monocular depth has no absolute scale, and the ceiling lights, curtains, dark window, wall boundaries and bottom-edge foreground are visibly over-smoothed or assigned implausible depths.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only a sparse subset of the scene: potted plants on the left in frames 1–2, a pot and chair near the middle-right, another potted plant and chair farther right, and people in frames 4–5; most walls, curtains, shelves, lamps and furniture remain unlabeled black. The masks clarify relative placement despite the dim RGB: the detected people are in front of the camera wearer, one near the lower centre-right and another farther right, with the frame-5 person closest and partly cut off at the bottom/right; the chairs and pots lie behind or beside them at roughly 1–3 m, whereas the people are approximately 0.5–2 m away. The increasing person-mask size from frame 4 to frame 5 is consistent with the person becoming nearer as the viewpoint turns right, while the separated plant and chair masks reveal objects that are partially blended into the background in RGB. The map is unreliable for complete geometry and inter-object distance because it misses most instances, truncates labels and masks, changes colours between person instances, and provides no depth ordering except what can be inferred from overlap and apparent size.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects a single yellow body skeleton in the fourth-frame region, positioned low and right of centre in front of the camera wearer; its torso is approximately upright, with the head above the shoulders and the limbs extending downward and sideways. Combined with RGB and depth, this person is roughly 1–2 m away, faces generally toward the camera wearer or slightly sideways, and is not clearly within the camera wearer’s arm reach; no reliable pose is shown for the much closer, partly out-of-view person in frame 5. The skeleton makes body orientation and joint arrangement easier to distinguish than in the blurred RGB, but it shows no magenta hand skeletons and gives no information about plants, chairs, walls or other spatial surfaces. It is unreliable for temporal change because only one of five frames has a pose, several limb segments appear distorted or incomplete, and gaze direction, exact facing angle, hand reach and occluded body parts cannot be determined confidently.
